questions.question: A matrix \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}\) satisfies \(P^3 - 4P^2 + 5P - 2I = 0\) where \(I\) is a \(3 \times 3\) identity matrix. The set of all possible eigenvalues of matrix \(P\) is .
questions.explanation:
Given that the matrix \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}\) satisfies the matrix polynomial equation: \[P^3 - 4P^2 + 5P - 2I = 0\] \[f(\lambda) = \lambda^3 - 4\lambda^2 + 5\lambda - 2 = 0\] We find the roots of this cubic equation by testing small integer values: If \(\lambda = 1\): \[f(1) = (1)^3 - 4(1)^2 + 5(1) - 2 = 1 - 4 + 5 - 2 = 0\] Since \(\lambda = 1\) satisfies the polynomial, \((\lambda - 1)\) is a factor. We perform polynomial long division or synthetic division to extract the remaining quadratic factor: \[\lambda^3 - 4\lambda^2 + 5\lambda - 2 = (\lambda - 1)(\lambda^2 - 3\lambda + 2) = 0\] Now, we factor the quadratic equation \(\lambda^2 - 3\lambda + 2 = 0\): \[\lambda^2 - 2\lambda - \lambda + 2 = 0\] \[\lambda(\lambda - 2) - 1(\lambda - 2) = 0 \implies (\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 2) = 0\] Combining all factors gives the complete characteristic factorization: \[(\lambda - 1)^2(\lambda - 2) = 0\] The roots of the equation are \(\lambda = 1, 1, 2\). Therefore, the set of all possible eigenvalues of matrix \(P\) is \(\{1, 2\}\), which corresponds to option (C). \[\boxed{\text{(C) $\{1,2\}$}}\]
Key points
  • Cayley-Hamilton Matrix Theorem: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic scalar polynomial equation \(|A - \lambda I| = 0\).

questions.question: Consider a matrix \[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\] Let \[\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\] and \[\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}\]. The number of solutions to the linear system of equations \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) is .
questions.explanation:
Given the non-homogeneous linear system of equations \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\), where: \[A = egin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \ -1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = egin{bmatrix} 1 \ 3 \ 0 \end{bmatrix}\] Initial augmented matrix \([A \mid \mathbf{b}]\): \[[A \mid \mathbf{b}] = \left[ egin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \ -1 & 1 & 0 & 3 \ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \end{array} ight]\] Step 1: \[R_2 o R_2 + R_1\] \[\left[ egin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 2 & 4 \ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \end{array} ight]\] Step 2: \[R_3 o R_3 - R_2\] \[\left[ egin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 2 & 4 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & -4 \end{array} ight]\]
  • \( ext{rank}(A) = 2\).
  • \( ext{rank}([A \mid \mathbf{b}]) = 3\).
Since \( ext{rank}(A) eq ext{rank}([A \mid \mathbf{b}])\), the system is inconsistent. Therefore, the total number of solutions is \(0\). \[ oxed{ ext{(A) 0}}\]
Key points
  • Rouché-Capelli Consistency Rule: A linear system \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) has zero solutions if and only if the augmented column parameters increase the vector subspace rank: \( ext{rank}(A) eq ext{rank}([A \mid \mathbf{b}])\).
  • Solution Classifications:
    • Unique Solution: \( ext{rank}(A) = ext{rank}([A \mid \mathbf{b}]) = n\) (where \(n\) is the number of variables).
    • Infinitely Many Solutions: \( ext{rank}(A) = ext{rank}([A \mid \mathbf{b}]) < n\).
    • No Solution: \( ext{rank}(A) eq ext{rank}([A \mid \mathbf{b}])\).

questions.question: Which one among the following statements is true for the function \(f(x) = x|x|\) ?
options: \(f(x)\) is discontinuous but not differentiable at \(x = 0\)
\(f(x)\) is continuous but not differentiable at \(x = 0\)
questions.explanation:
We are given the function: \[f(x) = x|x|\] Let us redefine the function by resolving the absolute value definition \(|x|\): \[|x| = \begin{cases} x, & \text{if } x \geq 0 \\ -x, & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}\] Thus, \(f(x)\) can be written as a piecewise function: \[f(x) = \begin{cases} x(x) = x^2, & \text{if } x \geq 0 \\ x(-x) = -x^2, & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}\] 1. Continuity Check at \(x = 0\)
  • Left-Hand Limit (LHL):
    \[\lim_{x \to 0^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 0^-} (-x^2) = 0\]
  • Right-Hand Limit (RHL):
    \[\lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (x^2) = 0\]
  • Function Value:
    \[f(0) = 0^2 = 0\]
Since \(\text{LHL} = \text{RHL} = f(0) = 0\), the function \(f(x)\) is continuous at \(x = 0\). 2. Differentiability Check at \(x = 0\)
Let us find the derivative \(f'(x)\) by differentiating the piecewise components: \[f'(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{d}{dx}(x^2) = 2x, & \text{if } x > 0 \\ \frac{d}{dx}(-x^2) = -2x, & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}\] Now evaluate the one-sided derivatives at \(x = 0\):
  • Left-Hand Derivative (LHD):
    \[f'(0^-) = \lim_{x \to 0^-} (-2x) = 0\]
  • Right-Hand Derivative (RHD):
    \[f'(0^+) = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (2x) = 0\]
Since \(\text{LHD} = \text{RHD} = 0\), the function \(f(x)\) is differentiable at \(x = 0\), and \(f'(0) = 0\). Therefore, \(f(x)\) is both continuous and differentiable at \(x = 0\). \[\boxed{\text{(d) }\ \ f(x)\text{ is continuous and differentiable at } x = 0.}\]

questions.question: Given \(f(x,y) = x^2 - 2xy + y^2\) The complete contour of the equation \(f(x,y) = 1\) is described by the option(s) .
options: An ellipse with length of major axis equal to 1
questions.explanation:
We are given the function: \[f(x, y) = x^2 - 2xy + y^2\] We need to find the complete contour described by the equation: \[f(x, y) = 1\] Substituting the expression for \(f(x, y)\): \[x^2 - 2xy + y^2 = 1\] Recognizing the left-hand side as a perfect square algebraic identity \(\left((x - y)^2 = x^2 - 2xy + y^2\right)\): \[(x - y)^2 = 1\] Taking the square root on both sides gives two possible linear equations: \[x - y = \pm 1\] This splits into two separate straight line equations:
  1. \(x - y = 1\) (Option A)
  2. \(x - y = -1\) (Option D)
Since this is a Multiple Select Question (MSQ), the complete contour is described collectively by both options A and D. \[\boxed{\text{A, D}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
Do not accidentally select only one option. When solving quadratic equations like \(u^2 = 1\), always remember to include both the positive and negative roots (\(u = \pm 1\)). Missing the negative root would lead to omitting option D.

questions.question:
Among the following, the differential equation(s) not representative of a linear dynamical system is/are .
  1. (i) \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}+2t\dfrac{dx}{dt}+x(t)=u(t)\)
  2. (ii) \(\left(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+2\dfrac{dx}{dt}+x(t)=u(t)\)
  3. (iii) \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}+2\dfrac{dx}{dt}+x(t)=u(t)\)
questions.explanation:
For a differential equation to represent a linear dynamical system,
  1. \textbf{1.} The dependent variable and all its derivatives must appear only to the first power \(\left(\dfrac{dx}{dt},\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}\right)\).
  2. \textbf{2.} There should be no products among the dependent variable and its derivatives \(\left(x\cdot\dfrac{dx}{dt},\ \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}\cdot\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right)\).
Checking given differential equations: (i)
\[\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + 2t\frac{dx}{dt} + x(t) = u(t)\] Here, \(x(t)\) and its derivatives appear linearly. The coefficient \(2t\) is a function of the independent variable \(t\). Hence, (i) is linear. (ii)
\[\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2 + 2\frac{dx}{dt} + x(t) = u(t)\] The term \(\left(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right)^2\) contains the derivative raised to the second power, violating the linearity condition. Hence, (ii) is nonlinear. (iii)
\[\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + 2\frac{dx}{dt} + x(t) = u(t)\] Here, \(x(t)\) and its derivatives appear linearly. The coefficient \(2\) is a constant. Hence, (iii) is linear. Therefore, only equation (ii) is not representative of a linear dynamical system. \[\boxed{\text{(C) (ii) only}}\]

questions.question: Given a differential equation \[\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}+x=0\ \text{with}\ x(0)\neq0.\] Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: \(|x(t)|^2 + \left|\dfrac{dx(t)}{dt}\right|^2 = c\) for all \(t\geq0,\) for some real constant \(c>0\)
questions.explanation:
Given the differential equation \[\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + x = 0,\qquad x(0)\neq 0\] This equation represents 'Simple Harmonic Oscillator' with \(\omega=1\). Hence, the general solution is \[x(t) = A\cos t + B\sin t,\] where \(A\) and \(B\) are constants determined by the initial conditions. Differentiating, \[\frac{dx}{dt} = -A\sin t + B\cos t\] Now evaluate the quantity appearing in the options: \[\begin{aligned} |x(t)|^2+\left|\frac{dx}{dt}\right|^2 &=(A\cos t+B\sin t)^2+(-A\sin t+B\cos t)^2 \\ &=A^2(\cos^2 t+\sin^2 t) +B^2(\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t) \\ &\quad +2AB\sin t\cos t -2AB\sin t\cos t \\ &=A^2+B^2. \end{aligned}\] Thus, \[|x(t)|^2+\left|\frac{dx}{dt}\right|^2=A^2+B^2=c,\] which is a constant for all \(t\ge 0\). Since \(x(0) = A\neq 0,\) we have \[A^2 + B^2 > 0\] Therefore, the constant satisfies \(c>0\). Hence, \[|x(t)|^2+\left|\frac{dx}{dt}\right|^2 = c,\ \forall\, t\ge 0,\ \text{for some real constant}\ c>0\] \[\boxed{\text{(B)}\ |x(t)|^2+\left|\frac{dx}{dt}\right|^2 = c,\, \text{for all}\ \, t\ge 0,\, \text{for some real constant}\ c>0}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume that \(B\) must be nonzero; only \(A=x(0)\neq 0\) is guaranteed.

questions.question: Consider a function \(f(z) = z^2 + z + 1\) where \(z \in \mathbb{C}\) is a complex variable. A simple closed contour \(\gamma\) in \(z\)-plane encloses the point \(z = 1 + 0j\). The value of integral \(\oint_{\gamma} \frac{f(z)}{z-1} \, dz =\) .
questions.explanation:
Given the function: \[f(z) = z^2 + z + 1\] We need to evaluate the contour integral: \[I = \oint_{\gamma} \frac{f(z)}{z - 1} \, dz = \oint_{\gamma} \frac{z^2 + z + 1}{z - 1} \, dz\] where \(\gamma\) is a simple closed contour enclosing the point \(z = 1 + 0j = 1\). The integrand has a simple pole at \(z = 1\). Since the contour \(\gamma\) explicitly encloses the point \(z = 1\), this pole lies inside the region bounded by \(\gamma\). According to Cauchy's Integral Formula, if a function \(f(z)\) is analytic within and on a simple closed contour \(\gamma\), and \(a\) is a point inside \(\gamma\), then: \[\oint_{\gamma} \frac{f(z)}{z - a} \, dz = 2\pi j \cdot f(a)\] Here, \(a = 1\). Evaluating \(f(z)\) at \(z = 1\): \[f(1) = 1^2 + 1 + 1 = 3\] Substituting \(f(1)\) back into the formula: \[I = 2\pi j \cdot f(1) = 2\pi j \cdot 3 = 6\pi j\] Thus, the value of the integral is \(6\pi j\). \[\boxed{A. \ 6\pi j}\]
Key points
  • Cauchy's Integral Formula: \(\oint_{\gamma} \frac{f(z)}{z - a} \, dz = 2\pi j \cdot f(a)\) when the point \(a\) lies inside the contour \(\gamma\).
  • If the singularity lay outside the contour, the integral would be \(0\) by Cauchy's Integral Theorem.

questions.question: A box contains three apples and two oranges. Two fruits are removed randomly in succession. The probability that the first is an apple and the second is an orange is_______.
questions.explanation: Probability that the first fruit is an apple: \[P(A_1)=\frac{3}{5}\] After removing one apple, remaining fruits are: \[2 \text{ apples and } 2 \text{ oranges}\] Hence, probability that the second fruit is an orange: \[P(O_2|A_1)=\frac{2}{4}=\frac{1}{2}\] Therefore, \[P(A_1\cap O_2)=P(A_1)\times P(O_2|A_1)\] \[=\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{1}{2}\] \[=\frac{3}{10}\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) }\frac{3}{10}}\]

A square wave of frequency \(20\,\text{kHz}\) contains the fundamental frequency and odd harmonics: \[f,\;3f,\;5f,\ldots = 20\,\text{kHz},\;60\,\text{kHz},\;100\,\text{kHz},\ldots\] The ideal low-pass filter has cut-off frequency \(f_c=21\,\text{kHz}\). questions.question: Given two signals:\[x(t)=u(t-2)-u(t-3)\]and\[y(t)=e^{-4t}u(t).\]If\[z(t)=x(t)*y(t),\]then \(Z(s)\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2cm}}\).
questions.explanation:
Theory: Convolution in the time domain corresponds to multiplication in the Laplace domain. Given,\[x(t)=u(t-2)-u(t-3),\]and \[y(t)=e^{-4t}u(t).\]The Laplace transform of \(x(t)\) is \[X(s) = \frac{e^{-2s}}{s} - \frac{e^{-3s}}{s} = \frac{e^{-3s}(e^{s}-1)}{s}.\]Also, \[Y(s) = \frac{1}{s+4}.\]Since \[z(t)=x(t)*y(t),\]we have \[Z(s)=X(s)Y(s).\]Hence, \[Z(s) = \frac{e^{-3s}(e^{s}-1)}{s(s+4)}.\]Using \[e^{-3s}(e^{s}-1) = e^{-2s}-e^{-3s},\]the expression is already in simplified form. \[\boxed{\text{(A): }\displaystyle \frac{e^{-3s}(e^{s}-1)}{s(s+4)}}\]
Key points
  • \(\mathcal{L}\{u(t-a)\}=\dfrac{e^{-as}}{s}\).
  • Convolution in time becomes multiplication in the Laplace domain.
  • Always compute \(X(s)\) and \(Y(s)\) separately before multiplying.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use the Laplace transform of \(e^{-4t}\) without including the unit-step function.
  • Do not confuse convolution with multiplication in the time domain.
  • While simplifying exponentials, verify identities such as \(e^{-3s}(e^{s}-1)=e^{-2s}-e^{-3s}\).

questions.question: A common gate amplifier represents a .
questions.explanation: A common-gate amplifier has Low input impedance (\(R_{in} \approx \dfrac{1}{g_m}\)) and High output impedance (\(R_{out}\approx R_D\)) Hence, it senses an input current without significantly loading the source and delivers an output current to the load. The current gain is \[A_i = \frac{I_{\text{out}}}{I_{\text{in}}} \approx 1.\] Thus, \[I_{\text{out}} \approx I_{\text{in}}.\] A Current Controlled Current Source (CCCS) is a dependent source in which the output current is controlled by the input current. A CCCS has low input impedance so that it can easily sense the input current without causing a significant voltage drop at the input. It has high output impedance so that the output current remains nearly constant and is almost independent of the load resistance, thereby behaving as an ideal current source. Hence, the common-gate amplifier is modeled as a Current Controlled Current Source (CCCS). Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }\text{Current Controlled Current Source}}\]

questions.question: In the following active filter circuit with ideal op-amps, \(R\) is \(1\text{ k}\Omega\), \(C\) is \(1\ \mu\text{F}\), and \(V_{\text{in}}\) has an amplitude of \(1\text{ V}\) at \(1000\text{ rad/s}\). The amplitude of \(V_{\text{out}}\) is V.
questions.explanation:
The circuit consists of three cascaded inverting stages with an additional feedback path from \(V_{out}\) to the first summing node. For \(R=1\,\text{k}\Omega\) and \(C=1\,\mu\text{F}\), \[RC=10^{-3}\,\text{s}, \qquad \omega RC=1000\times10^{-3}=1\] The first stage has feedback impedance \[Z_f=R\parallel\frac{1}{sC}=\frac{R}{1+sRC}\] Hence, \[V_{o1}=-\frac{1}{1+sRC}\left(V_{in}+V_{out}\right)\] The second stage is an inverting integrator, \[V_{o2}=-\frac{1}{sRC}V_{o1}\] The third stage is an inverting amplifier of gain \(-1\), \[V_{out}=-V_{o2}=\frac{V_{o1}}{sRC}\] Combining, \[V_{out}\left[(sRC)^2+sRC+1\right]=-V_{in}\] At \(\omega RC=1\), we have \(sRC=j\), \[\frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} =-\frac{1}{j^2+j+1} =-\frac{1}{j}=j\] Therefore, \[\left|\frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}\right|=1\] Since the amplitude of \(V_{in}\) is \(1\,\text{V}\), \[|V_{out}|=1\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) }1.0\,\text{V}}\]
Key points
  • An inverting integrator has gain \(-\dfrac{1}{sRC}\).
  • At \(\omega RC=1\), substitute \(sRC=j\).

questions.question: A 16-bit processor has 16-bit wide instructions and a few internal registers. Every 16-bit instruction is encoded in a fixed format with one operation code of 7 bits and up to three operands. The operand can be an internal register and each operand is encoded by 3 bits. All the internal registers can be specified in an instruction using 3 bits. The correct statements for this processor is/are :
options: The processor can support 128 unique operation codes (Opcodes).
The processor has up to 8 internal registers.
The processor can support 512 unique operation codes (Opcodes).
questions.explanation:
Given: Each operand is encoded using 3 bits, and the opcode field is 7 bits.
  • Statement (A) is incorrect: 16 registers would require \[\log_2 16 = 4\,\text{bits}\] but only 3 bits are available for each operand.
  • The number of unique opcodes representable using a 7-bit opcode field is: \[2^7 = 128\] Option (B) is correct.
  • The number of internal registers that can be specified using a 3-bit operand field is: \[2^3 = 8\] Therefore, the processor has at most 8 internal registers. Option (C) is correct.
  • Statement (D) is incorrect: 512 opcodes would require \[\log_2 512 = 9\,\text{bits}\] while only 7 bits are provided for the opcode field.
\[\boxed{B\;,\; C}\]
Key points
  • An \(n\)-bit field can encode exactly \(2^n\) distinct values; this applies uniformly to register addressing, opcode selection, or any other binary-encoded field.
  • The number of bits required to represent \(M\) distinct values is \(\lceil \log_2 M \rceil\); this is the inverse relationship used to verify whether a given field size is sufficient.
Mistakes to avoid
  • When checking if a claimed value (e.g., 16 registers or 512 opcodes) fits within a given field, always compute \(\log_2(\text{claimed value})\) and compare it to the available bit-width, rather than checking \(2^{\text{bits}}\) against the claimed value loosely.
  • Do not assume operand bits and opcode bits are interchangeable; they are separate fields within the instruction word serving different purposes.

questions.question: A straight thin wire carrying a current of \(I = 1\text{A}\) in the direction \(\hat{n} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{i} - \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{j} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{k}\) is placed inside a magnetic field of \(\vec{B} = (2\hat{i} + 2\hat{k})\,\text{T}\). The force per unit length of the wire is _____ \(\text{N/m}\).
questions.explanation:
The differential force equation yields: \[\bar{F} = I d\bar{\ell} \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{x} + \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{y} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{z} \right) \times (2\hat{x} + 2\hat{z})\] Evaluating the cross product using determinants: \[= \begin{vmatrix} \hat{x} & \hat{y} & \hat{z} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \end{vmatrix}\] \[= \hat{x}\left(\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}} - 0\right) - \hat{y}\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} - \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\right) + \hat{z}\left(0 - \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\right)\] \[= \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{x} - \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{z}\] \[\bar{F} = d\bar{\ell}\left( \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{x} - \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{z} \right)\] \[\frac{\bar{F}}{d\bar{\ell}} = \left( \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{x} - \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{z} \right)\] \[\boxed{\text{C) $\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{x} - \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{z} $}}\]
Key points
  • The magnetic force on a differential current element is computed using the vector cross product of the direction vector and the magnetic field vector.

A single phase transformer has a rating of \(10\text{kVA}\), \(50\text{Hz}\), \(1100\text{V}/220\text{V}\). In an open circuit test with the high voltage side open, the following are obtained:
  • Voltage applied to the low voltage winding \(= 220\text{V}\)
  • Measured power \(= 363\text{W}\)
  • Measured current \(= 2.75\text{A}\)
Magnetizing reactance \(X_\text{m}\) referred to the high voltage winding is _____ \(\Omega\).
questions.explanation: Given parameters: \[\cos\phi = \frac{P}{VI} = \frac{363}{220 \times 2.75} = 0.6\] The magnetizing current component is: \[I_m = I_0 \sin\phi = 2.75 \times 0.8 = 2.2\,\text{A}\] The magnetizing reactance \(X_m\) relative to the low-voltage side is: \[X_m = \frac{V}{I_m} = \frac{220}{2.2} = 100\,\Omega\] Referred to the high-voltage side, the magnetizing reactance becomes: \[X_m' = \frac{X_m}{K^2} = \frac{100}{\left(\dfrac{220}{1100}\right)^2}\] \[= \left(\frac{1100}{220}\right)^2 \times 100 = 2500\,\Omega\] \[\boxed{2500}\]

questions.question: Exacerbate : Mitigate :: ________ Choose the option with the correct pair of words to fill the blank.
questions.explanation:
We need to find the word pair whose relationship mirrors the baseline analogy *Exacerbate : Mitigate*. Let us define the core semantic relationship linking these two verbs:
  • Exacerbate: To make a problem worse, more severe, or to intensify a negative state.
  • Mitigate: To make a problem less severe, serious, or to alleviate a negative state.
The baseline relationship follows an **antonym pair** structure where both words operate along the same scalar dimension (the severity or intensity of a problem). We evaluate each option against this exact framework:
  • Option A (Aggravate : Alleviate): *Aggravate* means to worsen or intensify a problem (synonymous with *exacerbate*), while *alleviate* means to make a problem less severe or relieve it (synonymous with *mitigate*). This perfectly replicates the antonym relationship along the identical semantic axis.
  • Option B and C: *Precipitate* means to cause something to happen suddenly or prematurely, which fails to track the direct antonym axis of *mitigate*.
  • Option D (Emancipate : Exonerate): Both words carry distinct positive legal meanings (*emancipate* means to set free; *exonerate* means to absolve from blame), meaning they are not antonyms.
Therefore, Option A is the uniquely correct parallel pair. \[\boxed{\text{A. Aggravate : Alleviate}}\]
Key points
  • The relationship is a parallel matching antonym set: \(\text{Exacerbate} \approx \text{Aggravate}\) and \(\text{Mitigate} \approx \text{Alleviate}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Avoid selecting pairs based solely on generic positive or negative connotations; the target choice must mirror the precise action-oriented antonym axis of the prompt.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Four people P, Q, R, and S, of different ages, make the following observations. P -- I am younger than S. Q -- I am neither the youngest nor the oldest. R -- P is older than me. Based on these observations, the youngest person is _____.
questions.explanation:
From the given logical statements, we need to determine who is the youngest individual among P, Q, R, and S. We break down the relational constraints and inequalities from each statement (where higher value indicates older age):
  1. P's Statement: \(P < S\) (P is younger than S).
  2. R's Statement: \(R < P\) (R is younger than P).
  3. Chaining the Inequalities: Combining these two structural relations gives the ordering chain: \[R < P < S\]
  4. Q's Statement: Q states that he is neither the youngest (\(\min\)) nor the oldest (\(\max\)).
Let us analyze where Q can be placed within the established chain \(R < P < S\). Since Q cannot be the absolute youngest or oldest, Q cannot be placed to the left of R or to the right of S. Q must fit somewhere within the internal bounds of the sequence, meaning \(R < Q\) and \(Q < S\). Regardless of whether Q is older or younger than P, R remains bounded at the absolute minimum position of the ordering chain under all valid permutations. Therefore, R is strictly the youngest individual. This logical derivation matches Option C. \[\boxed{\text{C. R}}\]
Key points
  • Chaining linear inequalities allows you to establish definitive minimum and maximum boundary elements across a dataset.
  • Boundary constraints like ``neither min nor max'' eliminate items from extreme positions without needing to fix their exact internal rank.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not waste time trying to find the exact relative age rank between P and Q; their internal positioning has no mathematical effect on identifying the absolute minimum boundary element.

questions.question: ``He often _______ the numbers. False claims are not going to help. Honesty _______ trust'', said the manager. Choose the option with the correct order of words to fill the blanks.
questions.explanation:
We need to determine the correct pair of words to logically complete the manager's statement regarding transparency and corporate metrics. An analysis of the first sentence segment, ``He often the numbers. False claims are not going to help,'' indicates that the individual alters or inflates numeric values, as established by the negative context of ``false claims.'' The verb exaggerates fits this meaning directly. Looking at the second sentence segment, ``Honesty trust,'' the statement expresses a foundational principle where being honest acts as a structural catalyst that creates or gives rise to trust. The verb engenders means precisely to cause, produce, or give rise to a feeling or situation. Evaluating the alternatives:
  • Option A (exaggerates; engenders): Fits both contextual positions perfectly.
  • Option B (excels; encourages): The phrase ``excels the numbers'' is grammatically incorrect.
  • Option C (aggravates; alleviates): ``Aggravates the numbers'' does not fit the semantic context.
  • Option D (diminishes; eliminates): Contradicts the sentence logic because honesty does not eliminate trust.
Hence, Option A is the uniquely consistent choice. \[\boxed{\text{A. exaggerates; engenders}}\]
Key points
  • Exaggerate means to represent something as being larger, greater, or better than it really is.
  • Engender is a precise verb signifying to cause or breed a specific systemic condition.

questions.question: Charity : P :: Retaliation : Q Choose the appropriate pair of words P and Q that fit the analogy.
questions.explanation:
We need to find the pair of words \((P, Q)\) that satisfies the double analogy relation: \[\text{Charity} : P :: \text{Retaliation} : Q\] Establishing the core semantic relationships links a specific human behavior to its motivating character trait. Charity is an action driven by someone who is defined as magnanimous (generous, kind, and forgiving). Parallel to this, retaliation is an action driven by someone who is defined as vindictive (vengeful, spiteful, and seeking revenge). Testing the alternatives shows that Option A is incorrect because *parsimonious* means stingy, which is the opposite of charity. Option B is incorrect because *amicable* means friendly, which contradicts retaliation. Option C is incorrect because *resentful* is a temporary emotion rather than a character trait that matches the structural setup. Therefore, **Option D** (\(P = \text{Magnanimous}; \ Q = \text{Vindictive}\)) is the only pair that completes the parallel analogy layout. \[\boxed{\text{D. P = Magnanimous; Q = Vindictive}}\]
Key points
  • The analogy maps an action to its defining character trait: \(\text{[Action]} : \text{[Adjective describing the actor]}\).

We need to find the antonym of the word protagonist. A protagonist is defined as the leading character, hero, or principal figure in a novel, play, or story. Conversely, an antagonist is a person who actively opposes or is hostile to someone or something; in literature, it represents the principal adversary of the protagonist. Evaluating the remaining options:
  • Aagnostic: A person who believes that nothing is known or can be known of the existence or nature of God.
  • Carsonist: A person who deliberately sets fire to property.
  • Danarchist: A person who rebels against any authority, established order, or ruling power.
Hence, Option B is the direct antonym. \[\boxed{\text{B. antagonist}}\]

questions.question: `When the teacher is in the room, all students stand silently.' If the above statement is true, which one of the following statements is not necessarily true?
options: If any student is not standing silently, then the teacher is not in the room.
When the teacher is in the room, all students are silent.
If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.
When the teacher is in the room, all students are standing.
questions.explanation:
Given the true conditional premise: ``When the teacher is in the room, all students stand silently,'' we need to identify which statement is not necessarily true. Let us express the prompt statement in standard propositional logic notation: * Let \(P\) = The teacher is in the room. * Let \(Q\) = All students stand silently. The premise states that \(P \implies Q\) is **True**. Let us analyze the logical validity of each option:
  • Option A: ``If any student is not standing silently, then the teacher is not in the room.'' This translates to \( eg Q \implies eg P\), which is the **contrapositive** of our premise. A contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original implication statement, so this is strictly True.
  • Option B: ``When the teacher is in the room, all students are silent.'' This is a restatement of \(P \implies Q\), which is explicitly True.
  • Option C: ``If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.'' This translates to \(Q \implies P\), which is the **converse** of our premise. The truth of an implication does not guarantee the truth of its converse (affirming the consequent). Thus, this is not necessarily true.
  • Option D: ``When the teacher is in the room, all students are standing.'' This is a valid direct restatement of the conditional premise, so it is strictly True.
Hence, Option C is not necessarily true. \[ oxed{ ext{ C. If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.}}\]
Key points
  • Given a true implication \(P \implies Q\), its contrapositive (\( eg Q \implies eg P\)) is guaranteed to be true, while its converse (\(Q \implies P\)) and inverse (\( eg P \implies eg Q\)) are logical fallacies and not necessarily true.

questions.question:
Combinatorics deals with problems involving counting. For example, ``How many distinct arrangements of N distinct objects in M spaces on a circle are possible?'' is a typical problem in combinatorics. This kind of counting is sometimes used in the modeling of several physical phenomena. Often, in such models, the different combinatorial possibilities are assigned probability values. Assigning probabilities enables the computation of the average values of physical quantities. Consider the following statements:
  • P: Combinatorics is always invoked in the modeling of physical phenomena.
  • Q: Modeling some physical phenomena involves assigning probabilities to combinatorial possibilities in order to compute average values of physical quantities.
Based on the passage above, what can be inferred about statements P and Q?
options: P is False and Q is False
P is False and Q is True
P is True and Q is False
P is True and Q is True
questions.explanation:
Based on the text passage regarding combinatorics and physical modeling, we need to determine the truth values of statements P and Q. Let us analyze the text to evaluate each statement:
  • Statement P: ``Combinatorics is always invoked in the modeling of physical phenomena.'' The text states that combinatorics is ``sometimes used in the modeling of several physical phenomena.'' The absolute qualifier **always** in statement P overextends this claim, making statement P **False**.
  • Statement Q: ``Modeling some physical phenomena involves assigning probabilities to combinatorial possibilities in order to compute average values of physical quantities.'' The text explicitly notes: ``Often, in such models, the different combinatorial possibilities are assigned probability values. Assigning probabilities enables the computation of the average values of physical quantities.'' This matches statement Q directly, making it **True**.
Therefore, P is False and Q is True, which corresponds to Option B. \[\boxed{\text{ B. P is False and Q is True}}\]
Key points
  • Critical reading requires distinguishing between absolute constraints (e.g., *always*, *must*) and partial conditions (e.g., *sometimes*, *often*) mentioned in text passages.

questions.question: `When it is raining, peacocks dance.' Based only on this sentence, which one of the following options is necessarily true?
options: Peacocks dance only when it is raining.
When peacocks dance, it is raining.
When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.
When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.
questions.explanation:
Given the conditional premise statement: ``When it is raining, peacocks dance,'' we need to identify which statement is necessarily true. Let us express the premise statement using propositional logic operators: * Let \(R\) = It is raining. * Let \(D\) = Peacocks dance. The prompt statement means that the implication \(R \implies D\) is **True**. Let us analyze the logical validity of the choices:
  • Choice A: ``Peacocks dance only when it is raining.'' This maps to \(D \implies R\) (the converse), which is a logical fallacy and not necessarily true.
  • Choice B: ``When peacocks dance, it is raining.'' This is another restatement of the converse \(D \implies R\), which is not necessarily true.
  • Choice C: ``When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.'' This translates directly to \( eg D \implies eg R\), which is the **contrapositive** of our premise. Since a conditional statement and its contrapositive are always logically equivalent, this statement is strictly True.
  • Choice D: ``When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.'' This maps to \( eg R \implies eg D\) (the inverse), which is not necessarily true.
\[ oxed{ ext{C. When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.}}\]
Key points
  • For any fundamentally true implication \(P \implies Q\), its conditional contrapositive (\( eg Q \implies eg P\)) is always logically guaranteed to be true.

questions.question: Water : P :: Food : Q Choose the P and Q combination from the options below to form a meaningful analogy.
questions.explanation:
We need to find a combination for \((P, Q)\) that completes the double analogy: \(\text{Water} : P :: \text{Food} : Q\). Let us analyze the biological relationship linking each substance to its matching physiological sensation:
  • Water is consumed to relieve the physical sensation of Thirst.
  • Food is consumed to relieve the physical sensation of Hunger.
This establishes a parallel relationship, where each substance acts as the direct counter-agent to satisfy a specific physiological need. Setting \(P = \text{Thirst}\) and \(Q = \text{Hunger}\) creates a perfectly balanced double analogy along identical biological axes. \[\boxed{\text{A. P = Thirst; Q = Hunger}}\]
Key points
  • Analogy structures require maintaining an identical relationship axis (Substance : Corresponding Deprivation Sensation) across both comparison pairs.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: `The shopkeeper sells lemons.' In this sentence, the word `lemons' is the ________.
questions.explanation:
We need to identify the grammatical function of the word `lemons' in the sentence: ``The shopkeeper sells lemons.'' Let us break down the functional parts of the clause:
  • Subject: ``The shopkeeper'' (the agent performing the action).
  • Verb: ``sells'' (the action being performed).
  • Object: ``lemons'' (the entity receiving the direct action of the verb).
This matches A. \[\boxed{\text{A. object}}\]
Key points
  • A direct object is a noun or pronoun that directly receives the action of a transitive verb, answering the question what? or whom?.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: `If Anish had scored hundred runs in today's match, he would have been made the captain of his team. He would have then become the youngest captain in his team's history. Unfortunately, he got out without scoring any runs. Hence, there won't be any change in the captaincy for now.' Based on the paragraph above, which one of the following statements is true?
options: Anish made hundred runs but was denied captaincy.
Anish was the captain of his team before the game today.
The current captain is older than Anish.
Anish is the youngest player in his team.
questions.explanation:
Based on the provided biographical text segment regarding team selection criteria, we evaluate the statements to identify which claim is strictly true. Let us cross-examine each option against the facts established in the paragraph:
  • The text presents a conditional scenario: *If* Anish had scored a century, he *would* have become the captain and been the youngest captain in history.
  • However, the text explicitly reveals what actually happened: ``Unfortunately, he got out without scoring any runs. Hence, there won't be any change in the captaincy for now.''
  • This confirms that the current captain remains in office, and because Anish would have broken a history record as the youngest candidate had he succeeded, it logically follows that the current, un-displaced captain must be older than him.
This matches statement C. \[\boxed{\text{C. The current captain is older than Anish.}}\]
Key points
  • Subjunctive conditional statements (e.g., ``If he had...'') describe hypothetical scenarios; factual tracking must rely on the direct, unconditional assertions in the text.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: `The team _____ more than 300 runs in 20 overs _______ rains. However, some players needed to improve their batting skills.' Choose the option with the correct sequence of words to fill the blanks.
questions.explanation:
We need to choose the correct sequence of words to fill the blanks in the sentence: ``The team more than 300 runs in 20 overs rains.'' Let us analyze each clause contextually:
  • First Blank: The sentence concludes with a descriptive statement in the past tense (``some players needed to improve...''). Therefore, the initial independent clause must be in the simple past tense to maintain narrative consistency. This isolates scored.
  • Second Blank: The sentence introduces a counter-premise (rains). The preposition despite means ``notwithstanding'' or ``in spite of'' and perfectly transitions a noun phrase without a helping verb.
This corresponds to C. \[\boxed{\text{C. scored; despite}}\]
Key points
  • Prepositions like despite or in spite of function to introduce a contrastive noun phrase, whereas conjunctions like although require a complete subordinate clause.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: ‘All the mangoes in the basket are good.' If the above statement is false, then which one of the following statements is necessarily true?
options: All the mangoes in the basket are not good.
No mango in the basket is good.
In the basket, some of the mangoes are good and some are not good.
There exists at least one mango in the basket that is not good.
questions.explanation:
Given that the universal affirmative statement ``All the mangoes in the basket are good'' is **False**, we need to find which statement is logically guaranteed to be necessarily true. In predicate logic, the negation of a universally quantified statement (``All \(X\) are \(Y\)'') is structurally equivalent to an existential statement asserting the opposite condition (``There exists at least one \(X\) that is not \(Y\)''): \[\neg \Big[ \forall x \in M, \text{Good}(x) \Big] \equiv \exists x \in M, \neg\text{Good}(x)\] Let us evaluate the choices based on this negation rule:
  • Choice A and B require *all* or *none* of the mangoes to change states simultaneously, which is an over-negation and not necessarily true.
  • Choice C asserts that *some are good and some are not*, which cannot be guaranteed.
  • Choice D states: ``There exists at least one mango in the basket that is not good.'' This matches the existential negation rule perfectly.
This matches D. \[\boxed{\text{D: There exists at least one mango in the basket that is not good.}}\]
Key points
  • The strict logical negation of ``All items satisfy a condition'' is simply ``At least one individual item does not satisfy the condition.''

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about four numbers:
  • (S1) The average of the four numbers is 25
  • (S2) Each number is at most 40
  • (S3) Each number is at least 20
Choose the option that is necessarily correct.
questions.explanation:
We need to determine the logical implication relationship between three statistical statements regarding a set of four numbers: * (S1) The average of the four numbers is \(25\). * (S2) Each number is at most \(40\). * (S3) Each number is at least \(20\). Let us test the sufficiency of combining (S1) and (S3) to see if they imply statement (S2):
  • From (S1), if the average of the four elements \(\{a, b, c, d\}\) is \(25\), their total sum must equal: \[a + b + c + d = 4 \times 25 = 100\]
  • From (S3), each individual number has a strict lower floor limit of \(20\) (\(a, b, c, d \ge 20\)).
  • To find how large any single number (say, \(a\)) can possibly be, we minimize the other three numbers to their absolute lowest allowable limits (\(b = c = d = 20\)): \[a + 20 + 20 + 20 = 100\] \[a + 60 = 100 \implies a_{\text{max}} = 40\]
Since the maximum possible value for any element under these constraints is exactly \(40\), every single number is guaranteed to be at most \(40\). This matches statement (S2) perfectly. Therefore, (S1) and (S3) together imply (S2). This matches choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. (S1) and (S3) together imply (S2)}}\]
Key points
  • To maximize a specific element within a fixed sum system, compress all remaining component values down to their absolute minimum boundary floors.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: ‘People are crowding around ____ pit into which ____ elephant has fallen. I have never seen an elephant looking more bewildered ____ miserable. Here it is in a most undignified position, thrust into a pit and made to look up ____ a vast, curiosity-stricken crowd.' Choose the option with the correct sequence of words to fill the blanks.
questions.explanation:
We need to select the correct sequence of words to fill the four blanks in the provided textual passage. Let us evaluate each blank sequentially based on English grammar and syntax rules:
  1. First Blank: ``People are crowding around pit...'' Since the text refers to a specific, unique pit containing the elephant, it requires the definite article the.
  2. Second Blank: ``...into which elephant has fallen.'' The noun begins with a vowel sound, requiring the indefinite article an.
  3. Third Blank: ``...looking more bewildered miserable.'' This links two coordinate adjectives describing the elephant's condition, requiring the conjunction and.
  4. Fourth Blank: ``...made to look up a vast... crowd.'' This functions as a preposition indicating direction or focus toward an target object, requiring at.
Combining these choices yields the sequence: the; an; and; at. This maps to choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B: a; an; and; at}}\]
Key points
  • Singular nouns starting with vowel sounds require the article an, while descriptive coordinates are joined together using the conjunction and.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Among the following options, the antonym of the word `nocturnal' is _____.
questions.explanation:
We need to find the antonym of the word nocturnal. The word nocturnal describes organisms or phenomena that are active or occur strictly during the night. Its direct biological antonym is diurnal, which describes organisms that are active during the day. The remaining choices do not fit this specific axis: normal and abnormal are antonyms regarding regularity, and exceptional means unusual or outstanding. \[\boxed{\text{B. diurnal}}\]
Key points
  • Biological lifecycle vocabulary uses the paired terms nocturnal (night-active) and diurnal (day-active).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Each one of the following clues contains a keyword that is partially filled. Clue 1: Synonym of recognize (8 letters): _D_NT_FY Clue 2: A story long enough to fill a book (5 letters): _ _ _ EL Clue 3: Two of something (6 letters): _ _ _ PLE Clue 4: A fraction of something, split equally into two parts (4 letters): _ _ _ F The first letter of each of the keywords can be rearranged to form a four-letter word. Which one of the options below is a possible choice for the four-letter word?
questions.explanation:
We need to solve four word clues, collect their first letters, and rearrange them to form a valid four-letter word. Let us decode each word clue systematically using the letter length and keyword constraints:
  • Clue 1 (Synonym of recognize, 8 letters): Matches IDENTIFY. First letter = I.
  • Clue 2 (A story long enough to fill a book, 5 letters): Matches NOVEL. First letter = N.
  • Clue 3 (Two of something, 6 letters): Matches COUPLE. First letter = C.
  • Clue 4 (A fraction of something, split equally into two parts, 4 letters): Matches HALF. First letter = H.
We collect the first letters from our solutions: {I, N, C, H}. Rearranging this set of letters to match the options yields the valid English word CHIN. \[\boxed{\text{A. CHIN}}\]
Key points
  • Letter puzzle systems are resolved by finding unique synonyms that match the given blank templates before performing an anagram rearrangement.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Verbosity: Brevity :: Insolence: ________ Choose the word that best fills the blank.
questions.explanation:
We need to determine the correct word to complete the double analogy: \(\text{Verbosity} : \text{Brevity} :: \text{Insolence} : \underline{\hspace{1.5cm}}\). Let us analyze the relationship defining the baseline pair:
  • Verbosity means using more words than needed, whereas brevity means concise and exact use of words in writing or speech. This forms an explicit antonym relationship.
  • Insolence is defined as rude, disrespectful, and arrogant behavior. The direct semantic antonym for insolent behavior is showing deference, politeness, or respect.
Evaluating the alternatives: Innocence is the lack of guilt, Solace means comfort in times of distress, and Wealth relates to material abundance. None of these function as direct antonyms to rudeness. \[\boxed{\text{B. Respect}}\]
Key points
  • Word pair analogies depend on establishing a crisp contextual axis (e.g., negative behavior characteristic vs. positive behavioral corrective).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: `If his latest movie had been a commercial success, the actor would have made enough money to sponsor his next movie.' Based only on the above sentence, which one of the following statements is true?
options: The actor will certainly sponsor his next movie.
His latest movie was a commercial success.
The actor made enough money from his latest movie.
His latest movie was not commercially successful.
questions.explanation:
Given the conditional premise statement: ``If his latest movie had been a commercial success, the actor would have made enough money to sponsor his next movie,'' we need to find which statement is factually true. Let us analyze the grammar structure of this sentence:
  • The sentence uses the third conditional form (``If + past perfect..., would have + past participle...'').
  • The third conditional is explicitly reserved for describing hypothetical past scenarios that did not happen. It expresses an alternative counterfactual timeline.
  • Therefore, the real-world factual state is the exact opposite of the conditional premise components: the movie was *not* a commercial success, and consequently, the actor did *not* make enough money.
Reviewing the choices shows that Choice D directly matches this factual reality. \[\boxed{\text{D. His latest movie was not commercially successful.}}\]
Key points
  • Subjunctive past expressions (``If it had been...'') signal that the event described in the antecedent clause is factually false in reality.

We need to select the correct sequence of prepositions to complete the sentence: ``My friend and I parted the door the cabin that I had rented the night.'' Let us evaluate the required spatial and temporal prepositions step-by-step:
  1. First Blank: ``parted … the door''. The verb parted used in a spatial context means separated or said goodbye at a specific local point, requiring the directional preposition at.
  2. Second Blank: ``the door … the cabin''. This indicates a relationship of belonging or structural containment between the door and the cabin, requiring the genitive preposition of.
  3. Third Blank: ``rented … the night''. This marks a specific intended duration of time for the rental agreement, requiring the temporal preposition for.
Combining these choices yields the sequence: at; of; for. This maps to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. at; of; for}}\]
Key points
  • Idiomatic preposition selection requires matching localized coordinates (at a location), belonging relationships (of an object), and duration markers (for a duration).

To continue the progression, the missing seventh tile must have a total dot count of: \[3 + 5 = 8 \text{ dots}\] Evaluating the choices for a total dot count of \(8\):

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Consider an art gallery whose walkways are shown as lines in the diagram. A black dot represents a junction of two walkways. A guard may be placed at a junction to watch over the walkways that join at that junction. The minimum number of guards needed to watch all the walkways is ____.
questions.explanation:
We must find the minimum number of guards placed at junctions such that every walkway (edge) has at least one of its endpoints guarded. This is equivalent to modeling the **minimum vertex cover** problem on a graph. A vertex cover is a set of vertices such that every edge in the graph is incident to at least one vertex in the set. We can evaluate this graph system through direct construction and optimization constraints:
  • Degree-Based Analysis: Placing guards at the highest-degree junctions maximizes the simultaneous coverage of convergent walkways.
  • Trial and Elimination Bounds: Attempting to cover the network layout using only \(2\) guards consistently leaves at least one isolated walkway completely unmonitored. This sets a strict lower optimization bound of \(\ge 3\).
  • Optimal Placement Configuration: Selecting the three principal intersecting high-degree junctions successfully intercepts all edges across the graph, demonstrating that exactly \(3\) guards provide complete network security.
This minimal configuration matches Option B. \[\boxed{\text{B. 3}}\]
Key points
  • The art-gallery guard layout problem on a discrete network reduces to a minimum vertex cover graph optimization.
  • For networks belonging to bipartite spaces, König's theorem establishes that the minimum vertex cover cardinality matches the maximum matching size (\(|V_{\text{cover}}| = |M_{\text{max}}|\)).
Mistakes to avoid
  • A guard stationed at vertex \(v\) monitors *all* convergent pathways connected to \(v\); do not mistake this for a guard standing inside a single walkway.
  • Avoid over-counting shared edges, as a single optimal guard placement can satisfy up to four edge covers simultaneously.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The \(2^{\text{nd}}\) of June is a Thursday in a certain year. Which day of the week is the \(3^{\text{rd}}\) of July in that year?
questions.explanation:
Given that June 2 is a Thursday, we need to calculate the corresponding day of the week on July 3. We compute the exact calendar day using modular date arithmetic by counting the total number of days spanning the interval from June 2 to July 3: \[\text{Days remaining in June after June 2} = 30 - 2 = 28\text{ days}\] \[\text{Total calendar offset days to July 3} = 28 + 3 = 31\text{ days}\] We reduce this total net shift modulo \(7\) to determine the number of complete weeks and remaining extra days: \[31 = (4 \times 7) + 3 \implies 31 \equiv 3 \pmod 7\] An advance of \(31\) days is equivalent to shifting exactly \(3\) days forward from Thursday: \[\text{Thursday} \xrightarrow{+1} \text{Friday} \xrightarrow{+1} \text{Saturday} \xrightarrow{+1} \text{Sunday}\] This calculation corresponds to Option D. \[\boxed{\text{Option D. Sunday}}\]
Key points
  • The month of June always contains exactly 30 days.
  • Adding an offset of 31 days to a starting day of the week is equivalent to shifting forward by 3 days (\(\equiv +3 \pmod 7\)).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Avoid off-by-one errors; the total distance from June 2 to July 3 spans exactly 31 discrete day counts, not 32.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A coin with heads facing up is shown as H; and a coin with tails facing up is shown as T;. Six coins are placed in the Starting Arrangement, as shown in the figure below. A ``step'' is defined as interchanging a pair of adjacent coins without flipping them. The minimum number of steps needed to go from the Starting Arrangement to the Final Arrangement, as shown in the figure, is
questions.explanation:
We are given an initial sequence of 6 coins and need to determine the minimum number of adjacent swaps (steps) required to transform the starting arrangement into the final target arrangement:
  • Starting Arrangement: \(\text{H}_1 \; \text{H}_2 \; \text{H}_3 \; \text{T}_1 \; \text{T}_2 \; \text{T}_3\)
  • Final Arrangement: \(\text{T}_1 \; \text{T}_2 \; \text{T}_3 \; \text{H}_1 \; \text{H}_2 \; \text{H}_3\)
Step 1: Understand the adjacent swap property
A single step interchanges two adjacent coins. In terms of relative positions, one single adjacent swap can change the relative order of at most one \((\text{H}, \text{T})\) pair. Step 2: Calculate total required pair inversions
In the starting arrangement, every Heads (\(\text{H}\)) coin is located to the left of every Tails (\(\text{T}\)) coin:
  • There are \(3\) Heads coins (\(\text{H}\)) and \(3\) Tails coins (\(\text{T}\)).
  • Each of the \(3\) Heads coins must end up to the right of all \(3\) Tails coins.
Therefore, each \(\text{H}\) coin must cross past all \(3\) \(\text{T}\) coins independently: \[\text{Total Inversions} = (\text{Number of H coins}) \times (\text{Number of T coins})\] \[\text{Total Inversions} = 3 \times 3 = 9\] Step 3: Minimum steps verification
Since each adjacent swap resolves exactly \(1\) inversion between an \(\text{H}\) and a \(\text{T}\), the absolute minimum number of steps needed is equal to the total number of inversions: \[\text{Minimum Steps} = 9\] This corresponds to choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 9}}\]
Key points
  • The minimum number of adjacent element swaps required to transform an array is strictly bounded by the total number of inversions.
  • Tagging identical-looking items with unique sub-indices ensures that the permutation sequence is tracked accurately.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume the total swap cost equals the raw number of coins that are out of place; local adjacent movement constraints scale with element displacement distance.

questions.question: A paper shown in Panel I is folded along the dashed lines (- - -) to construct a cube. The shaded regions shown in Panel I appear on the outer surface of the cube. Referring to cubes shown in Panel II, which one of the options is correct?
options: Only (i) can correspond to the unfolded cube in Panel I.
Only (ii) can correspond to the unfolded cube in Panel I.
Both (i) and (ii) can correspond to the unfolded cube in Panel I.
Neither (i) nor (ii) can correspond to the unfolded cube in Panel I.
questions.explanation:
A flat paper net containing shaded regions (Panel I) is folded into a 3D cube. We need to determine which of the assembled cube choices in Panel II matches the net. We analyze the geometry and face adjacency constraints of the flat net layout:
  1. Opposite Face Verification: In any standard cube net, faces separated by exactly one intervening square fold to become opposite, non-adjacent faces in 3D space. Tracking the shaded faces shows they are separated by a face in the net, meaning they must occupy **opposite parallel sides** on the folded cube.
  2. Evaluating Cube (i): This configuration displays the two shaded faces on adjacent perpendicular sides, which directly violates the opposite-face constraint. This layout is physically impossible.
  3. Evaluating Cube (ii): This configuration positions the shaded faces on the correct opposite parallel sides while preserving the exact relative geometric orientation of the shading patterns along the folded edges.
Thus, only cube (ii) can be successfully constructed from the net, corresponding to Option B. \[\boxed{\text{B. Only (ii) can correspond to the unfolded cube in Panel I}}\]
Key points
  • Alternating faces along any linear track of a flat cube net fold to become opposite parallel faces in 3D space.
  • Always verify the relative edge orientation of asymmetric shading blocks along the fold boundaries to eliminate mirrored distractors.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not merely check if the correct faces are shaded; tracking the spatial adjacency and whether faces are perpendicular or parallel is critical.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
In a population, patients who have high cholesterol also have high blood-pressure (BP). Some patients with high BP also have diabetes. There are no patients who have both high cholesterol and diabetes. Furthermore,
  1. the total number of patients with at least one of these conditions is \(75\),
  2. the number of patients with high cholesterol is \(10\),
  3. the number of patients with high BP is \(45\), and
  4. the number of patients with only high BP and no other conditions is \(20\).
Then the number of patients who have both diabetes and high BP is ________.
questions.explanation:
Let \(C\) represent high cholesterol, \(B\) represent high blood pressure (BP), and \(D\) represent diabetes. We map the problem constraints and population values to direct set intersections:
  • Subset inclusion condition: \(C \subseteq B \implies C \cap B = C\) and \(|C \cap B| = |C| = 10\).
  • Disjoint condition: \(C \cap D = \emptyset \implies\) no patient can have both cholesterol and diabetes.
  • Cardinality parameters: \(|C| = 10, \quad |B| = 45, \quad |C \cup B \cup D| = 75, \quad |\text{only } B| = 20\).
We want to find the number of patients with both BP and diabetes, which is represented by the intersection cardinality \(x = |B \cap D|\). Since \(C\) is nested entirely inside \(B\), and \(C\) has zero overlap with \(D\), the total set \(B\) can be partitioned into three mutually disjoint regions: \[B = (\text{only } B) \cup (C \cap B) \cup (B \cap D)\] We substitute the known regional cardinalities into this total sum formula: \[45 = 20 + 10 + x\] \[45 = 30 + x \implies x = 15\] Therefore, the number of patients in the intersection \(|B \cap D|\) is exactly \(15\), matching Option B. \[\boxed{\text{B. 15}}\]
Key points
  • The constraint \(C \subseteq B\) reduces a complex three-set Venn layout to a simpler nested structure where \(C\) is a subset of \(B\), and \(D\) intersects \(B\) without touching \(C\).
  • Partitioning sets into disjoint regions allows calculation using basic linear addition.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not add \(|B| + |C|\) to find the union population if \(C \subseteq B\); since all elements of \(C\) are already inside \(B\), their union simplifies to \(|C \cup B| = |B| = 45\).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Circles \(C_1\), \(C_2\), and \(C_3\), with centers \(O_1\), \(O_2\), and \(O_3\), and radii \(r_1\), \(r_2\), and \(r_3\), respectively, touch each other as shown in the following figure.
Given \(r_1 = 2\text{ cm}\), \(r_2 = 1\text{ cm}\) and the angle \(\angle O_1O_3O_2\) is \(90^\circ\), \(r_3 =\) ________ \(\text{cm}\).
questions.explanation:
Three circles with radii \(r_1=2\text{ cm}\), \(r_2=1\text{ cm}\), and unknown radius \(r_3\) are mutually externally tangent, forming a right angle \(\angle O_1O_3O_2 = 90^\circ\) at center \(O_3\). Because the three circles are mutually externally tangent, the distance between any two centers equals the sum of their respective radii. This defines the side lengths of triangle \(\triangle O_1O_3O_2\): \[O_1O_2 = r_1 + r_2 = 2 + 1 = 3\] \[O_1O_3 = r_1 + r_3 = 2 + r_3\] \[O_2O_3 = r_2 + r_3 = 1 + r_3\] Since \(\angle O_1O_3O_2 = 90^\circ\), the side \(O_1O_2\) is the hypotenuse. We apply the Pythagorean theorem directly to this right-angled triangle: \[O_1O_2^2 = O_1O_3^2 + O_2O_3^2\] \[3^2 = (2 + r_3)^2 + (1 + r_3)^2\] We expand both binomial terms using \((a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\): \[9 = (4 + 4r_3 + r_3^2) + (1 + 2r_3 + r_3^2)\] \[9 = 2r_3^2 + 6r_3 + 5\] Rearranging this into a standard quadratic equation \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\) yields: \[2r_3^2 + 6r_3 - 4 = 0 \implies r_3^2 + 3r_3 - 2 = 0\] We solve for \(r_3\) using the quadratic formula \(r_3 = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\): \[r_3 = \dfrac{-3 \pm \sqrt{3^2 - 4(1)(-2)}}{2(1)} = \dfrac{-3 \pm \sqrt{9 + 8}}{2} = \dfrac{-3 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}\] Since a radius must be a positive real number (\(r_3 > 0\)), we reject the negative root and take the positive solution: \[r_3 = \dfrac{-3 + \sqrt{17}}{2}\] This matches Option A. \[\boxed{\text{A. } \frac{-3 + \sqrt{17}}{2}}\]
Key points
  • When two circles of radii \(r_i\) and \(r_j\) touch externally, the line segment connecting their centers has a length of exactly \(r_i + r_j\).
  • The vertex hosting the \(90^\circ\) angle defines the opposite side as the hypotenuse for setting up the Pythagorean equation.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Hypotenuse Selection Error: Ensure you place \(O_1O_2\) as the isolated hypotenuse term, as mistakenly treating \(O_1O_3\) or \(O_2O_3\) as the hypotenuse will yield an incorrect quadratic equation.
  • Always discard negative roots when solving for physical geometric dimensions like length or radius.

A school has 100 students distributed among \(1^{\text{st}}\) to \(10^{\text{th}}\) standards.
Based on this, which one of the following statements is always correct?
options: There are at least 10 students who belong to the same standard.
There is at least one student in each standard.
There are at most 10 students in \(10^{\text{th}}\) standard.
The total number of students from \(1^{\text{st}}\) to \(5^{\text{th}}\) standards is at least 50.
questions.explanation:
A school has \(100\) students distributed among \(10\) distinct standards (from 1st to 10th standard). We need to determine which statement is guaranteed to be true under all distributions. Let the \(100\) students be the ``pigeons'' and the \(10\) standards be the ``pigeonholes'' (\(n = 100\), \(k = 10\)). According to the Generalized Pigeonhole Principle, at least one pigeonhole must contain at least: \[\left\lceil \dfrac{n}{k} \right\rceil = \left\lceil \dfrac{100}{10} \right\rceil = 10 \text{ students}\] Therefore, it is mathematically guaranteed that **there are at least 10 students who belong to the same standard**, matching Option A. We can invalidate the remaining options by providing simple counter-examples: for Option B, we could place all 100 students into the 1st standard, leaving the other standards empty (\(0\) students). For Option C, all 100 students could be inside the 10th standard, violating ``at most 10 students''. For Option D, we could place 0 students in standards 1 to 5 and all 100 students in standards 6 to 10. \[\boxed{\text{A. there are at least 10 students who belong to the same standard}}\]
Key points
  • The Generalized Pigeonhole Principle states that if \(n\) items are put into \(k\) boxes, at least one box contains \(\ge \lceil n/k \rceil\) items.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed using three distinct single digit prime numbers?
questions.explanation:
We need to find how many 3-digit numbers can be formed using three distinct single-digit prime numbers. First, identify the single-digit prime numbers less than 10, which form the set \(S = \{2, 3, 5, 7\}\), giving exactly 4 available prime digits. Next, choose 3 distinct digits from these 4 options, which can be done in \(\binom{4}{3} = 4\) ways. Finally, arrange these 3 chosen distinct digits to form a 3-digit number. Since the digits must be unique within each number, the number of permutations for 3 distinct elements is \(3! = 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6\) arrangements. Computing the total combinations yields: \[\text{Total Numbers} = \binom{4}{3} \times 3! = 4 \times 6 = 24\] This matches Option B. \[\boxed{\text{B. 24}}\]
Key points
  • The single-digit primes are strictly \(2, 3, 5\), and \(7\). Note that \(1\) is not a prime number.
  • The calculation can also be modeled as selecting positions without replacement: \(4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24\).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: In a group of students, 10 students like Mathematics, 12 students like English, 4 students like both Mathematics and English, and 6 students like neither Mathematics nor English. The number of students in the group is ________.
questions.explanation:
We need to calculate the total number of students in a group based on their subject preferences. Let \(M\) be the set of students who like Mathematics, and \(E\) be the set of students who like English. The problem provides the following parameters: \(|M| = 10\), \(|E| = 12\), \(|M \cap E| = 4\), and the number of students who like neither subject is \(|(M \cup E)'| = 6\). We find the total number of students who like at least one of the two subjects (\(|M \cup E|\)) using the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion: \[|M \cup E| = |M| + |E| - |M \cap E|\] \[|M \cup E| = 10 + 12 - 4 = 22 - 4 = 18\] Adding the students who like neither subject gives the total population of the group: \[\text{Total Students} = |M \cup E| + |(M \cup E)'| = 18 + 6 = 24\] This corresponds exactly to Option C. \[\boxed{\text{C. }24}\]
Key points
  • Total Population formula: \(N = |M| + |E| - |M \cap E| + \text{Neither}\).
  • Breaking down the independent regions directly: Only Math \(= 6\), Only English \(= 8\), Both \(= 4\), Neither \(= 6\). Total \(= 6 + 8 + 4 + 6 = 24\).

questions.question: A paper shown in Panel I is folded along the dashed lines (- - - - -) to construct a cube. The shaded regions shown in Panel I appear on the outer surface of the cube. Referring to cubes shown in Panel II, which one of the options is correct?
options: Only (i) can correspond to the unfolded cube in Panel I.
Only (ii) can correspond to the unfolded cube in Panel I.
Both (i) and (ii) can correspond to the unfolded cube in Panel I.
Neither (i) nor (ii) can correspond to the unfolded cube in Panel I.
questions.explanation:
A paper net containing shaded regions (Panel I) is folded along its dashed lines to form a 3D cube. We need to determine which of the folded configurations in Panel II is physically possible. Analyzing the flat net layout in Panel I shows that the net consists of a central column of 4 squares with two side arms. Notice the square containing a shaded diamond design; when the net is folded into a cube, this face is surrounded by specific neighboring pattern alignments. Looking at the two triangles that meet at a shared fold line, these shaded sections join together to form a single solid block. In **Cube (i)**, the shaded diamond face shares an edge with a half-shaded face where the shaded triangle aligns with the corner of the diamond, matching the net folding rules. In **Cube (ii)**, the relative orientation of the shaded half-face is mirrored and flipped compared to how the edges meet in the net, making it physically impossible. Therefore, **Only (i)** can correspond to the unfolded net in Panel I, which matches Option A. \[\boxed{\text{A. Only (i) can correspond to the unfolded cube in Panel I}}\]
Key points
  • Faces that are separated by exactly one square on a flat net always fold to become *opposite* faces on a 3D cube.
  • Pay close attention to how the vertices of shaded shapes touch the shared fold lines to rule out mirrored options.

questions.question: Consider the cube shown below with its 8 corners labelled a, b, c, d, e, f, g, and h. The figure is representative. All corners are to be colored such that any two corners that are connected by an edge must be of different colors. The minimum number of colors required to achieve this is ___.
questions.explanation:
We need to find the minimum number of colors required to color the 8 corners of a cube such that any two corners connected by an edge have different colors. This is equivalent to finding the **chromatic number** \(\chi(G)\) of a cube graph. A graph can be colored using exactly 2 colors if and only if it contains no odd-length cycles (cycles of length 3, 5, 7, etc.), which defines it as a **bipartite graph**. Analyzing the cycles formed by the vertices and edges of a cube shows that every face of the cube forms a cycle of length 4 (\(a \to b \to h \to e \to a\)). Any paths that traverse the cube completely always require an even number of steps to return to a starting vertex. Since all cycles in a cube graph have an even length, the graph contains no odd cycles and is strictly bipartite. We can explicitly verify this by assigning two alternating colors to the vertices: Top face: Set \(a = \text{Color 1} \implies b = \text{Color 2}, \ c = \text{Color 2}, \ d = \text{Color 1}\). Bottom face: Set \(e = \text{Color 2} \implies f = \text{Color 1}, \ g = \text{Color 2}, \ h = \text{Color 1}\). Checking all 12 edges confirms that no two adjacent corners share the same color. Therefore, the minimum number of colors required is exactly **2**, matching Option D. \[\boxed{\text{D. }2}\]
Key points
  • The hypercube graph \(Q_3\) (a standard 3D cube structure) is a 3-regular bipartite graph.
  • The chromatic number of any non-empty bipartite graph is always exactly 2.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Four hills H1, H2, H3, and H4 are present in an area. The following observations are made about them:
  1. Neither H2 nor H3 is the easternmost hill.
  2. Neither H2 nor H3 is the westernmost hill.
  3. Neither the easternmost hill nor the westernmost hill is the southernmost hill.
  4. Two hills are located to the west of H2.
  5. The southernmost hill has at least two hills to its east.
The southernmost hill is ______.
questions.explanation:
We need to determine which hill is located furthest south based on a set of geographical observations. Let us map the constraints sequentially: Rule 1 states that neither \(H_2\) nor \(H_3\) is the easternmost or westernmost hill. This means \(H_2\) and \(H_3\) must occupy the middle positions along the East-West axis, while the outer boundaries are held by \(H_1\) and \(H_4\). Rule 2 states that neither the easternmost nor westernmost hill is the southernmost hill. Since \(H_1\) and \(H_4\) hold the boundaries, they cannot be southernmost, meaning the southernmost hill **must be either \(H_2\) or \(H_3\)**. Rule 3 states that two hills are located to the west of \(H_2\). Since there are 4 hills in total, \(H_2\) must be the 3rd hill from the west. Since \(H_3\) must occupy a middle position, it is placed as the 2nd hill from the west, creating the layout sequence: \(\text{West} \ [H_1/H_4] \to H_3 \to H_2 \to [H_4/H_1] \ \text{East}\). Rule 4 states that the southernmost hill has at least two hills to its east. Checking our candidates shows that \(H_2\) only has one hill to its east, which violates this rule, while \(H_3\) has two hills (\(H_2\) and the eastern boundary hill) to its east. Therefore, \(H_3\) must be the southernmost hill, which matches Option C. \[\boxed{\text{C. } H_3}\]
Key points
  • Rule 2 eliminates the outer boundary elements (\(H_1, H_4\)) from being the southernmost hill.
  • Combining the West-to-East positioning from Rule 3 with the eastern count requirement in Rule 4 uniquely isolates \(H_3\).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: As shown in the figure, circle \(C_{1}\) with center \(O_{1}\) and radius \(r_{1}\) touches the square \(VWXY\) at points \(P\) and \(Q\) while circle \(C_{2}\) with center \(O_{2}\) and radius \(r_{2}\) touches the square \(VWXY\) at points \(R\) and \(S\). The two circles touch each other at \(T\). Given \(r_{1}=1\text{ cm}\) and \(\overline{VY}=\overline{VW}=4\text{ cm}\), \(r_2 =\) ______ \(\text{cm}\).
questions.explanation:
As shown in Fig. Q26.2.10, circle \(C_1\) with center \(O_1\) and radius \(r_1 = 1\text{ cm}\) is tangent to two adjacent sides of a square \(VWXY\) of side length \(s = 4\text{ cm}\). Circle \(C_2\) with center \(O_2\) and radius \(r_2\) is tangent to the other two sides of the square. The two circles are externally tangent to each other at point \(T\). We need to calculate the value of radius \(r_2\). Let us set up a coordinate geometry framework along the line of symmetry by projecting the lengths onto the main diagonal of the square, \(WY\). The total length of this diagonal is given by \(WY = s\sqrt{2} = 4\sqrt{2}\). Because the circles are tangent to the sides of the corners, their centers \(O_1\) and \(O_2\) lie directly on this line. We break the total diagonal length into three distinct collinear segments: the segment from corner \(W\) to center \(O_1\) is \(WO_1 = r_1\sqrt{2} = 1\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2}\); the segment between the two centers is \(O_1O_2 = r_1 + r_2 = 1 + r_2\) because they are externally tangent; and the segment from center \(O_2\) to the opposite corner \(Y\) is \(O_2Y = r_2\sqrt{2}\). Summing these segments along the straight line yields the continuity equation: \[WY = WO_1 + O_1O_2 + O_2Y\] \[4\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2} + (1 + r_2) + r_2\sqrt{2}\] Isolating the variable \(r_2\) allows us to solve the linear system systematically: \[4\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} - 1 = r_2(1 + \sqrt{2})\] \[3\sqrt{2} - 1 = r_2(\sqrt{2} + 1)\] \[r_2 = \dfrac{3\sqrt{2} - 1}{\sqrt{2} + 1}\] Multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the algebraic conjugate \((\sqrt{2} - 1)\) simplifies the rational expression: \[r_2 = \dfrac{(3\sqrt{2} - 1)(\sqrt{2} - 1)}{(\sqrt{2} + 1)(\sqrt{2} - 1)} = \dfrac{3(\sqrt{2})^2 - 3\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} + 1}{2 - 1}\] \[r_2 = \dfrac{6 - 4\sqrt{2} + 1}{1} = 7 - 4\sqrt{2}\] This derived analytical value matches Option C. \[\boxed{\text{C. } 7 - 4\sqrt{2}}\]
Key points
  • The distance from a square's corner to the center of a circle tangent to both intersecting sides is always \(r\sqrt{2}\).
  • Writing a geometric continuity equation along a line of symmetry (like the main diagonal) simplifies problems involving inscribed circles.

questions.question: The figure shows two 4-tile patterns. Either one or both of the patterns can be used any number of times and in any orientation to construct a new pattern. Which one of the options below cannot be constructed by using only these two 4-tile patterns assuming there are no overlaps among them?
questions.explanation:
We need to identify which of the given composite options cannot be constructed by using the two 4-tile blocks shown without overlaps. Let us analyze the dimensions and areas of our two primitive building blocks:
  • Block 1: A \(2 \times 2\) square block composed of 4 small units (area = 4).
  • Block 2: A \(4 \times 1\) linear block composed of 4 small units (area = 4).
Since any combination of these blocks must have a total area that is a multiple of 4, let us test the matrix areas of the target options:
  • Option A: A \(2 \times 4\) grid (area = 8 units). This can be formed using exactly two \(2 \times 2\) square blocks.
  • Option B: A \(3 \times 4\) grid (area = 12 units). This can be paved by placing three \(4 \times 1\) linear blocks horizontally on top of each other.
  • Option C: A \(3 \times 4\) grid (area = 12 units). To fill a grid with a odd dimension like 3 using only \(2 \times 2\) squares and \(4 \times 1\) rectangles, any horizontal placement of a \(4 \times 1\) block leaves a remaining \(2 \times 4\) area, which can be covered by two \(2 \times 2\) blocks. However, looking at the layout of Option C, it cannot be segmented into combinations of \(2 \times 2\) squares and \(4 \times 1\) rectangles without cutting a block.
  • Option D: A \(4 \times 4\) grid (area = 16 units). This can be perfectly formed using four \(2 \times 2\) blocks.
Therefore, the layout in Option C cannot be constructed. \[\boxed{\text{Option C}}\]
Key points
  • Tessellation constraints require checking both total area divisibility and localized boundary matching along grid lines.

questions.question: Consider a knock-out women's badminton singles tournament where there are no ties. The loser in each game is eliminated from the tournament. Every player plays until she is defeated or remains the last undefeated player. The last undefeated player is declared the winner of the tournament. If there are 64 players in the beginning of the tournament, how many games should be played in total to declare the winner of the tournament?
questions.explanation:
We need to find the total number of matches played in a single-elimination (knock-out) badminton tournament with 64 players. In any single-elimination tournament, every match played results in exactly one player being eliminated from the competition. To determine a single unique winner, all other players must be defeated exactly once.
  • Total number of players (\(N\)) = 64
  • Number of players to be eliminated (\(N - 1\)) = \(64 - 1 = 63\)
Since each match accounts for exactly 1 elimination, the total number of games required is: \[\text{Total Matches} = N - 1 = 64 - 1 = 63\] This matches Option C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 63}}\]
Key points
  • For any knock-out tournament structure with \(N\) participants, the total number of matches required to find a single winner is always exactly \(N - 1\), regardless of whether \(N\) is a power of 2 or if byes are handed out.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A student needs to enroll for a minimum of 60 credits. A student cannot enroll for more than 70 credits. The credits are divided amongst project and three distinct sets of courses namely, core courses, specialization courses, and elective courses. It is compulsory for a student to enroll for exactly 15 credits of core courses and exactly 20 credits of project. In addition, a student has to enroll for a minimum of 10 credits of specialization courses. The maximum credits of elective courses that a student can enroll for is________.
questions.explanation:
We want to maximize the elective course credits a student can take under a set of linear course enrollment constraints. Let the course credits be defined as: Core Courses (\(C\)), Project (\(P\)), Specialization (\(S\)), and Electives (\(E\)). We establish the optimization limits from the given constraints:
  • Credit boundaries: \(60 \le \text{Total Credits} \le 70\)
  • Compulsory fixed credits: \(C = 15, \quad P = 20\)
  • Specialization minimum bound: \(S \ge 10\)
The equation for total credit accumulation is: \[\text{Total} = C + P + S + E\] \[\text{Total} = 15 + 20 + S + E = 35 + S + E\] To find the absolute maximum value for elective credits (\(E_{\text{max}}\)), we set the total credit budget to its upper ceiling limit (\(\text{Total}_{\text{max}} = 70\)) and minimize the remaining independent specialization parameter to its lowest allowable floor (\(S_{\text{min}} = 10\)): \[70 = 35 + S_{\text{min}} + E_{\text{max}}\] \[70 = 35 + 10 + E_{\text{max}}\] \[70 = 45 + E_{\text{max}} \implies E_{\text{max}} = 70 - 45 = 25\] This corresponds to Option D. \[\boxed{\text{ D. 25}}\]
Key points
  • Linear Optimization Boundary Constraints: To maximize an individual variable within a bounded summation system, assign the total equation space to its maximum upper limit while minimizing all other variable component values to their respective lower floors.

questions.question: In Panel I of the figure below, the front view and top view of a structure are shown. Which one of the 3D structures shown in Panel II possesses the views shown in Panel I?
questions.explanation:
